# Recovering Speech from a Spectrogram

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** Phase retrieval — the STFT's overlap makes a magnitude-only spectrogram *redundant*, and the Griffin–Lim algorithm exploits that redundancy to resynthesise the waveform, phase and all.
**Chapter:** [7 — Time-Frequency Analysis](../chap7.qmd)

---

## Background

A spectrogram shows $|S(f,t)|$ — the **magnitude** of the STFT. The **phase** is thrown away, and with it, apparently, the waveform: you cannot invert a magnitude alone, since infinitely many signals share it… for a *single* window. This "phase problem" is famous well beyond audio — X-ray crystallography faces exactly it (detectors record only $|\mathcal F\{\rho\}|^2$ of the electron density), and half of structural biology hangs on working around it.

But the STFT has a loophole: **overlap**. With a hop of a quarter window, every sample of the signal is described by *four* different frames. A magnitude-only STFT then contains about **4× more numbers than the signal has samples** — it is massively redundant, and the redundancy carries phase information in disguise: neighbouring frames must agree about the samples they share, and only (nearly) one phase assignment lets them.

## Key idea

Not every array of numbers is a valid STFT. A valid one is **consistent**: inverse-transform it, forward-transform the result, and you get the same coefficients back. The **Griffin–Lim algorithm** (1984) finds the signal by alternating between the two constraints we have:

1. **Consistency projection**: $x \leftarrow \mathrm{ISTFT}(X)$, then $X \leftarrow \mathrm{STFT}(x)$ — snap to something a real signal could produce;
2. **Magnitude projection**: $X \leftarrow A\,e^{\,i\angle X}$ — keep the *given* spectrogram magnitudes $A$, keep only the phase from step 1.

Start from **random phase** and iterate. Each round the frames negotiate their shared samples a little better; after a couple hundred rounds, out comes intelligible speech from what began as pure noise-phase garbage.

The demo runs this on a 2.4 s catchphrase — Roman Reigns' *"Acknowledge me!"* (WWE), shouted over a live crowd — and makes the problem deliberately hard: only **50 % overlap**, barely *two* numbers per signal sample, half the redundancy a typical analysis would use. (The two limits frame the difficulty: at 75 % overlap the reconstruction is almost easy; with **no** overlap it is impossible — disjoint frames have nothing to negotiate, *any* phase is self-consistent, and the iteration fixes nothing.)

## Code

```python
import numpy as np, scipy.signal as sig

nper, hop = 1024, 512                      # 50% overlap -> only ~2x redundancy
nov = nper - hop
_, _, S = sig.stft(y, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)
A = np.abs(S)                              # the spectrogram: magnitude ONLY

X = A * np.exp(2j*np.pi*np.random.rand(*A.shape))     # start from random phase
for k in range(300):                                  # Griffin-Lim iterations
    _, x  = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)   # -> signal domain
    _, _, Sx = sig.stft(x, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov) # -> a CONSISTENT stft
    X = A * np.exp(1j * np.angle(Sx))                 # keep our magnitude,
                                                      # adopt the negotiated phase
_, x_rec = sig.istft(X, fs, nperseg=nper, noverlap=nov)    # recovered speech
```

The reconstruction carries the words, the shout, and the crowd — everything — with a residual "phasiness" that is the audible price of working at half redundancy: rerun the same code at 75 % overlap and it largely disappears. (Audio: a 2.4 s quotation from a WWE broadcast, used here for demonstration.)

Three honest notes. The recovered waveform is **not sample-identical** to the original — a global sign and small per-band phase rotations remain unconstrained, as a close look at panel (b) shows; what is recovered is the *sound*. Convergence is slow ($1/k$-ish), and modern text-to-speech long ago replaced Griffin–Lim with neural vocoders — but every one of them still learns to solve exactly this problem: spectrogram in, phase out. And the redundancy bookkeeping is worth stating plainly: at 50 % overlap the magnitude STFT holds ~2 numbers per signal sample, at 75 % ~4, at 0 % ~1 — and phase retrieval works precisely when that count exceeds one.
